event-def.name: The First Fleet
event-def.prompt: On 26 January 1788, eleven ships of the First Fleet under Governor Arthur Phillip come to anchor at Sydney Cove, on the Country of the Eora people, and the colony of New South Wales is proclaimed. Some fifteen hundred souls — convicts, marines, and officers — must now raise a settlement and feed themselves at the far end of the world.

effect.text: 26 January 1788: the First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove and the colony of New South Wales is proclaimed.

event-def.name: The Second Fleet
event-def.prompt: In 1790 the Second Fleet reaches Sydney, its convicts landed sick and dying after a voyage of shameful neglect — later remembered as the Death Fleet. The survivors are labour the struggling colony sorely needs, and more mouths it can barely feed.

effect.text: More transports arrive from Britain, bearing convict labour for the young colony.

event-def.name: The Merino Flock
event-def.prompt: In 1797 the first merino sheep are landed in the colony, their fine fleece prized on the London wool market — the seed of an industry that could one day underwrite the settlement's fortunes. Building up the flock will demand capital and good pasture. Do you invest in the merino, or leave its promise to keep for now?

effect.text: Merino sheep are landed — the colony's wool prospects rise.
The merino flock is left to graze; its promise will keep.

event-def.name: Drought
event-def.prompt: The rains fail and a harsh drought settles over the colony; the ground cracks, the waterholes fall, and the crops wither in the paddocks. There is little for it but to ration the stores and wait for the season to break.

effect.text: A harsh drought settles over the colony; the ground cracks and the crops wither.

event-def.name: Bushfire
event-def.prompt: A hot northerly wind drives bushfire through the district, and the flames race through timber and scrub faster than any team can beat them out. The settlers can only cut breaks, save what stock and stores they can, and let the fire burn itself out.

effect.text: Bushfires sweep through the district, driven by a hot northerly wind.

event-def.name: The Hawkesbury in Flood
event-def.prompt: Heavy rain sends the Hawkesbury — the colony's granary — over its banks, and the brown floodwaters carry off the season's grain from the riverside farms. The settlers salvage what seed and stock they can reach from the high ground.

effect.text: The Hawkesbury bursts its banks and the floodwaters take the season's grain.

event-def.name: A Good Season
event-def.prompt: The season turns kind — steady rain and warm sun — and the crops come in heavy across the district. The granaries fill, and with full stores the settlers' spirits and their confidence in the colony both rise.

effect.text: A bountiful season — the granaries fill and spirits lift.

event-def.name: The Whaling Station
event-def.prompt: Whales run thick in the bays through the winter season, and shore whaling offers the colony one of its first true exports — oil for the lamps and mills of Britain, and bone for the trade in London. A try-works can be raised on the headland to render the catch.

effect.text: A shore whaling station opens; oil and bone fetch a fine price in London.

event-def.name: Free Settlers
event-def.prompt: A ship brings free settlers — not convicts but men and women who have paid their own passage, seeking land and a new start under the southern sky. Some can be put straight to work on the land; others will need the colony's help to find their feet. How will you receive them?

effect.text: Free settlers step ashore, seeking land and a new start.
The colony rallies to help the new arrivals find their feet.

event-def.name: The Absconders
event-def.prompt: A party of convicts has absconded into the bush, some chasing rumours of a free settlement or an overland road to China beyond the mountains. The governor must choose: turn out the guard to hunt them down, or offer emancipation to any who return and take up honest work.

effect.text: A party of convicts absconds into the bush; the guard is turned out to recapture them.
Rather than pursue the absconders, the governor offers emancipation to those who return and work.

event-def.name: The End of Transportation
event-def.prompt: For half a century the eastern colonies have been built on the forced labour of transported convicts. Now Britain brings that traffic to a close — New South Wales in 1840, and the last of the penal settlements in the years that follow. The colonies stand at a threshold, free-settler societies turning toward free labour and the beginnings of self-government.

effect.text: The transportation of convicts to the eastern colonies ends; the settlements turn to free labour and self-government.

event-def.name: The Squatting Runs
event-def.prompt: Pastoralists drive their flocks far beyond the official limits of settlement, taking up vast runs across country long held and cared for by First Nations peoples. The wool clip swells and fortunes follow, but the runs press hard onto lands and waters under others' long custody. Will you let the runs spread unchecked, or bring them under licence?

effect.text: Squatters take up vast pastoral runs far beyond the settled districts; the wool clip swells.
The government issues depasturing licences to bring the squatters' runs under order.

event-def.name: The Wool Boom
event-def.prompt: Fine merino fleece from the colonies commands record prices on the London wool market, and the pastoral economy rides high on the sheep's back. London buyers clamour for every bale the colony can send. Will you ship the season's clip to market?

effect.text: Colonial merino fleece commands high prices on the London wool market; the clip ships out at a handsome return.

event-def.name: Into the Interior
event-def.prompt: This is the age of the great inland expeditions — Sturt, Leichhardt, Burke and Wills — pressing into a continent long travelled and known by First Nations peoples, yet uncharted on colonial maps. Backers urge you to fund a crossing, though the arid heart has already claimed the lives of those who dared it. Will you fund the expedition, or judge the cost too high for now?

effect.text: An expedition sets out to cross the interior; much country is charted, though the arid centre exacts a heavy toll.
The colony judges the interior crossing too costly and holds the expedition back for now.

event-def.name: The Gold Rush
event-def.prompt: Gold is struck at Bathurst, and then in fabulous quantity at Ballarat and Bendigo. Word races around the world; ships lie empty at the wharves as labourers, clerks, and sailors alike throw down their tools and rush for the fields. Will you throw the colony open to the diggings?

effect.text: Gold is struck at Bathurst, then Ballarat and Bendigo; the rush is on, and diggers pour onto the fields.

event-def.name: A Payable Field
event-def.prompt: Prospectors bring word of a rich, payable field within reach of the settlement — quartz reefs and alluvial wash that assay well. The crushers can be set running day and night if the colony commits to working it. Will you open the field?

effect.text: A rich payable field is opened near the settlement; the crushers run day and night.

event-def.name: The World Comes to the Diggings
event-def.prompt: The gold draws people from across the globe — from Britain and Ireland, from Europe and the Americas, and in great numbers from southern China. Shipload after shipload lands for the diggings, and within a single decade the population of the gold colonies more than triples. Will you welcome the new arrivals?

effect.text: Shiploads of new arrivals land for the diggings; the colonial population swells.

event-def.name: The Eureka Stockade
event-def.prompt: At Ballarat the diggers have burned their mining licences and thrown up a rough stockade, in protest at the heavy fee and the troopers' relentless licence hunts. They raise the flag of the Southern Cross and swear an oath to stand by one another and defend their rights. Will you concede reform, or order the troops to break the stockade by force?

effect.text: After the Eureka Stockade at Ballarat, the licence is abolished for the miner's right and the vote; the goldfields win a measure of democracy.
The troops storm the stockade at Ballarat; order is restored, but at a cost in blood and standing.

event-def.name: The Gold Escort Robbery
event-def.prompt: The roads down from the diggings are thick with bushrangers, and a consignment of escorted gold makes a tempting prize. This time the escort is ambushed and overpowered, and the gold is carried off into the ranges. The loss must be borne.

effect.text: Bushrangers hold up the gold escort on the road from the diggings and make off with the consignment.

event-def.name: Rail and Telegraph
event-def.prompt: The first steam railway opens between Melbourne and its port, and the first telegraph wire begins to hum. For the price of the outlay, passengers, freight, and news can move at a pace the colony has never known. Will you invest in the new lines?

effect.text: The first railway and telegraph lines open in the colonies; passengers, freight, and news begin to move at a new pace.

event-def.name: The Overland Telegraph
event-def.prompt: In 1872 a single iron wire is strung nearly two thousand miles from Adelaide to Darwin, where it meets the submarine cable running on to Java and London. A message that once took months by ship can now reach Britain in hours, drawing the scattered colonies closer together. Will you throw the colony's weight behind completing the line?

effect.text: The Overland Telegraph is completed from Adelaide to Darwin and joined to the submarine cable; the colonies now reach London in hours, not months.

event-def.name: The Broken Hill Lode
event-def.prompt: In the arid far west of New South Wales, a boundary rider's hunch proves out one of the richest silver, lead and zinc lodes on earth. Mines, smelters and a whole new town rise from the desert, and the great company that will bear the hill's name is founded on the strike. Do you commit the capital to work the lode?

effect.text: A vast silver-lead lode is proved at Broken Hill; the mines and smelters make fortunes and a new mining colony.

event-def.name: Frozen Meat for London
event-def.prompt: In 1880 the steamer Strathleven lands the first cargo of frozen Australian meat in London in sound condition, proving that refrigeration can carry colonial beef and mutton across the tropics to the British table. A vast new export market opens to the pastoral colonies. Will you invest in the freezing works and ship the trade?

effect.text: The first frozen meat cargoes reach London in good order; refrigeration opens the British market to colonial beef and mutton.

event-def.name: The Intercolonial Railways
event-def.prompt: The colonies push their trunk lines toward one another, but each is built to its own gauge, so passengers and freight must change trains at every border, the break-of-gauge muddle that will vex Federation for decades. Extending the line is costly, yet it binds the colonies and their markets closer. Do you fund the extension?

effect.text: A new trunk railway links the colonies further, though the differing gauges force a change of train at the border.
The colony defers the costly railway extension for another session of parliament.

event-def.name: Marvellous Melbourne
event-def.prompt: On the back of gold and easy credit, 1880s Melbourne swells into one of the richest cities in the world, its streets lined with grand banks and its land values climbing on feverish speculation. The boom is intoxicating, and few pause to ask how long it can last. Do you ride the land boom?

effect.text: Speculation and easy credit make 'Marvellous Melbourne' one of the richest cities in the world; land values soar.

event-def.name: The Bank Crash of 1893
event-def.prompt: The land boom collapses, and in 1893 a run on the banks shutters many of them across the colonies, wiping out ordinary depositors overnight. The colonies slide into a deep depression from which recovery will be slow and uneven. There is little to be done but weather the ruin.

effect.text: The land boom collapses and a run on the banks in 1893 closes many of them; depositors are ruined and the colonies fall into depression.

event-def.name: The Great Shearers' Strike
event-def.prompt: In 1891 the shearers of Queensland and the pastoral colonies walk off the runs over wages and the freedom to organise, and the dispute hardens into one of the fiercest labour struggles the colonies have known, the seedbed of a labour movement and a future Labor party. The pastoralists demand the wool be got in; the unions demand recognition. How will you meet the strike?

effect.text: The Great Shearers' Strike ends in a settlement; out of the shearers' unions grows a labour movement and, in time, a Labor party.
The strike is broken with non-union labour and mounted police; the clip comes in, but bitterness lingers on the runs.

event-def.name: Votes for Women in South Australia
event-def.prompt: In 1894 South Australia moves to grant women not only the vote but the right to stand for parliament, the first Australian colony to do so and among the first places anywhere in the world. Reformers and suffrage campaigners have carried the long argument, and the bill now awaits assent. Will you enact the reform?

effect.text: South Australia grants women the vote and the right to stand for parliament — the first Australian colony to do so, and among the first in the world.

event-def.name: The Federation Convention
event-def.prompt: After the Corowa conference and the popular federal leagues, delegates from the colonies gather in convention to draft a constitution for a Commonwealth of Australia. The framework of a federal nation, its parliament, its powers and its courts, is hammered out clause by clause. Will you send delegates and back the drafting?

effect.text: Delegates from the colonies meet in convention and draft a constitution for a federal Commonwealth of Australia.

event-def.name: The Federation Referendum
event-def.prompt: The draft constitution goes to the people, colony by colony, to be approved or rejected at the ballot box, a nation founded by popular vote rather than by conquest or crown. Everything now turns on whether the electors carry it, and a first attempt may fall short of the quota and need revising. Do you put the constitution to the people now, or amend the terms first?

option.label: Put it to the people now

effect.text: At referendum the colonies vote to approve the constitution and join the Commonwealth; the people carry Federation.
A first referendum falls short of the quota; the constitution is amended and put to the people again.

event-def.name: The Federation Drought
event-def.prompt: From the mid-1890s one of the severest droughts on record grips the continent; the Murray and Darling fall to a trickle, and sheep and cattle perish in their millions across the parched inland. The turn of the century brings ruin to the pastoral districts even as Federation draws near. There is nothing to do but endure the dry.

effect.text: The Federation Drought grips the continent; the rivers fall to a trickle and stock perish in their millions across the inland.

indian-nation-type.description: The Arrernte hold Country in the centre of the continent, around Mparntwe - the place the colonists called Alice Springs. Survival in the arid centre rests on detailed knowledge of water sources and the routes between them. Colonial expeditions and the Overland Telegraph Line of the 1870s cut directly through Arrernte Country, and the telegraph station became the town.

indian-nation-type.country: Broome and the west Kimberley coast
indian-nation-type.description: The Yawuru are the coastal people of the Broome region on the west Kimberley coast, their Country taking in mangroves, mudflats and the waters beyond. From the 1880s the pearling industry transformed the region, drawing workers from across Asia and the Pacific and relying heavily - and often coercively - on Aboriginal labour.

The Kulin are an alliance of neighbouring peoples - among them the Wurundjeri, Boonwurrung, Taungurung, Dja Dja Wurrung and Wadawurrung - whose Country covers Port Phillip and central Victoria. The 1835 arrival of settlers at the Yarra began a rapid dispossession. Kulin leaders, William Barak foremost among them, spent the following decades petitioning colonial governments for land and rights.

indian-nation-type.country: Sydney basin and coastal New South Wales
indian-nation-type.description: The Eora are the coastal people of the Sydney basin, on whose Country the First Fleet anchored in January 1788. Theirs was a marine economy - fishing from bark canoes, gathering shellfish along the harbour and its inlets. The arrival of the colony brought dispossession and a catastrophic smallpox epidemic within two years. Eora people remain in Sydney today.

The Larrakia are the saltwater people of the Darwin region, with Country covering the harbour, coast and nearby islands. Their long-standing trade and travel connections run along the northern coast. The founding of Palmerston, later Darwin, in 1869 placed a colonial port directly on Larrakia Country. They are known today as the traditional owners of Darwin.

The Yolŋu of north-east Arnhem Land traded with Macassan mariners from Sulawesi for centuries before British settlement - an established international trade in trepang that predates the colony by generations. Arnhem Land's remoteness meant colonial settlement reached Yolŋu Country later and less completely than the south-east, and Yolŋu communities retain a high degree of autonomy.

The Noongar are the people of the entire south-west corner of Western Australia, one of the largest Aboriginal cultural blocs on the continent. Their calendar divides the year into six seasons rather than four, tracking the south-west's distinct cycles of weather, plant and animal life. Noongar Country was taken up for farming and timber from the 1830s onward.

The Wangkatja peoples hold Country across the arid Western Australian interior and goldfields. Living in that country depends on precise knowledge of water - soaks, rock holes and springs - and of the routes between them. The gold rushes of the 1890s drove thousands of prospectors across that Country in a matter of years.
